# Investigation of Stimulated Dynamics of Abrikosov Vortices in High-Temperature Superconductors

## Methodology and General Approach

The mechanical method for investigating stimulated dynamics of Abrikosov vortices has proven to be a valuable experimental tool for studying relaxation phenomena occurring within the vortex matter of high-temperature superconductors. This technique allows researchers to probe the internal dynamics of the vortex lattice by monitoring the mechanical response of the system to external perturbations, providing insight into the fundamental processes governing vortex motion and reorganization within the superconducting material.

## Influence of Pulsed Magnetic Fields on Relaxation Dynamics

Through the application of this mechanical approach, it was established that pulsed magnetic fields exert a significant influence on the natural course of relaxation processes taking place within the vortex matter. Rather than proceeding along an undisturbed trajectory, the relaxation dynamics of the vortex system respond directly to the characteristics of the applied pulses, indicating that external magnetic field pulses can serve as an effective means of manipulating and probing the internal state of the vortex configuration.

## Threshold Phenomena Observed in HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ

A series of experiments conducted on HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ samples, employing pulses with systematically varied duration and amplitude, uncovered the existence of distinct threshold phenomena characterizing the response of the vortex system to these external stimuli. These experiments demonstrated that the vortex matter does not respond continuously or proportionally to all applied pulses; instead, the system exhibits a clear threshold behavior that separates two qualitatively different response regimes.

Specifically, it was found that pulses possessing durations below a certain critical threshold value produce no discernible effect on the ongoing relaxation process—the vortex system continues its relaxation behavior as though undisturbed by the pulse. In marked contrast, once the pulse duration exceeds this critical threshold, the vortex system responds with a pronounced stepwise change in the relaxing mechanical moment. This sharp transition between an unresponsive regime and a regime characterized by abrupt discontinuous change underscores the existence of a well-defined critical time scale governing the reorganization dynamics of the vortex lattice under pulsed magnetic field excitation.

## Characteristic Formation Time of the Vortex Lattice

Building upon these observations, the characteristic formation time of the Abrikosov vortex lattice in HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ was determined experimentally to be approximately 20 microseconds. This value represents a substantially longer timescale than what would be expected based solely on single-vortex dynamics—specifically, it exceeds by an order of magnitude the time required for the formation of an individual vortex in conventional type II superconductors. This significant discrepancy suggests that the formation of the complete vortex lattice structure in high-temperature superconductors involves complex collective processes that extend well beyond the simple superposition of individual vortex nucleation events, highlighting the cooperative nature of vortex matter organization in these materials.

# Relaxation Dynamics of Abrikosov Vortex Matter in HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ Under Pulsed Magnetic Fields

## Introduction

The dynamics of the Abrikosov vortex lattice in type-II superconductors remains a subject of significant interest, particularly regarding the characteristic timescales governing vortex formation, motion, and relaxation. Understanding these processes is crucial both for fundamental physics of mixed-state superconductivity and for practical applications where superconductors are subjected to rapidly varying magnetic fields. In this work, we employ a mechanical resonance-based technique to probe the stimulated dynamics of Abrikosov vortices in the high-temperature superconductor HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ (HoBCO), focusing specifically on how pulsed magnetic field perturbations of controlled duration and amplitude influence the subsequent relaxation of the vortex system.

## Methodology

The mechanical method used in this study exploits the coupling between the vortex lattice and the crystal lattice through pinning forces, allowing vortex dynamics to be inferred from mechanical oscillation measurements of the sample. A single crystal of HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ was mounted on a sensitive mechanical oscillator, and the sample was subjected to short magnetic field pulses superimposed on a static background field. By systematically varying the pulse duration (ranging from sub-microsecond to several tens of microseconds) and pulse amplitude, we were able to probe how these perturbations affect the subsequent creep and relaxation behavior of the vortex system, as reflected in changes to the mechanical response of the sample.

This approach offers a unique advantage over conventional magnetic relaxation measurements, as it provides direct mechanical access to the internal stress state of the vortex lattice, making it particularly sensitive to structural changes within the vortex ensemble that may not be readily apparent in bulk magnetization measurements.

## Results

Our measurements reveal a pronounced **threshold phenomenon** in the response of the vortex system to pulsed field excitations. Specifically, we find that magnetic field pulses shorter than a critical duration—approximately 20 microseconds—produce no measurable effect on the subsequent relaxation dynamics of the vortex lattice. Only pulses exceeding this threshold duration are capable of altering the relaxation process, manifesting as a change in the characteristic relaxation rate or mechanical response of the sample following the pulse.

This sharp threshold behavior stands in contrast to what would be expected if the vortex system responded proportionally to the total energy or momentum delivered by pulses of varying length. Instead, the existence of a well-defined critical pulse duration points to a discrete physical process that must be completed before the perturbation can meaningfully affect the collective vortex state.

## Discussion

We interpret this threshold behavior as reflecting the finite time required for the Abrikosov vortex lattice to reorganize into a new collective configuration in response to the applied perturbation. The observed threshold time of approximately 20 microseconds is therefore identified as the characteristic **formation time of the vortex lattice** as a whole—that is, the time necessary for the ensemble of vortices to establish a new correlated, quasi-equilibrium spatial arrangement.

Notably, this timescale is approximately one order of magnitude longer than the time required for the nucleation and formation of a *single* Abrikosov vortex in type-II superconductors, which is typically governed by the Ginzburg-Landau relaxation time and related microscopic processes occurring on the scale of microseconds or less. This discrepancy highlights an important distinction between the microscopic process of individual vortex nucleation and the mesoscopic/macroscopic process of collective lattice reorganization, which involves cooperative rearrangement of many interacting vortices subject to pinning, vortex-vortex interactions, and the underlying disorder potential of the material.

## Conclusion

These findings provide direct experimental evidence for a hierarchy of timescales in vortex matter dynamics, distinguishing the fast, local process of single-vortex formation from the slower, collective process of vortex lattice organization. The observed threshold phenomenon offers a new methodological tool for probing vortex lattice dynamics and lends support to theoretical descriptions of vortex matter as a collectively interacting system whose response to external perturbations cannot be reduced to the behavior of individual vortices alone. This work contributes to a more complete understanding of non-equilibrium vortex matter dynamics in high-temperature superconductors and may have implications for the design of superconducting devices operating under rapidly pulsed magnetic field conditions.

# Alexei Abrikosov and the Physics of Superconductivity

Alexei Alexeyevich Abrikosov (1928–2017) was a Soviet-American theoretical physicist whose work fundamentally reshaped our understanding of superconductivity. Born in Moscow, he trained under some of the greatest minds in Soviet physics, including Lev Landau, and went on to make discoveries that would eventually earn him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2003.

Abrikosov's most celebrated contribution came in 1957, when he predicted the existence of what are now known as Abrikosov vortices. Working within the theoretical framework established by Vitaly Ginzburg and Lev Landau, he demonstrated that certain superconductors—later classified as Type-II superconductors—could allow magnetic fields to penetrate their interior in a highly structured way. Rather than expelling all magnetic flux (as predicted by the simpler Meissner effect seen in Type-I superconductors), these materials permit magnetic field lines to pass through in discrete, quantized tubes, each surrounded by a vortex of circulating supercurrent.

This insight was revolutionary because it explained how certain superconducting materials could maintain their superconducting properties even in the presence of strong magnetic fields—a property essential for practical applications. With this theoretical foundation, engineers and physicists were later able to develop high-field superconducting magnets, which today are indispensable components in technologies ranging from MRI machines to particle accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider.

The significance of Abrikosov's work extended beyond its immediate technical implications. It represented a triumph of theoretical prediction preceding experimental confirmation—a hallmark of great physics. The vortex lattice he described, often called the "Abrikosov lattice," was later observed experimentally, arranging itself in a triangular pattern that beautifully confirmed his mathematical predictions.

Throughout his career, Abrikosov continued to contribute to condensed matter physics, including work on the theory of metals and the behavior of electrons in strong magnetic fields. In 1991, following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, he emigrated to the United States, where he continued his research at Argonne National Laboratory.

With his theoretical elegance and deep physical intuition, Abrikosov exemplified the best traditions of the Landau school of physics. His work remains a cornerstone of modern condensed matter theory, illustrating how abstract mathematical reasoning can yield insights with profound practical consequences—bridging the gap between pure theory and technologies that shape our modern world.

# Abstract

We report a systematic investigation of vortex dynamics in high-temperature superconductors using high-resolution mechanical torque magnetometry. Torque measurements were performed on single-crystal samples across a range of temperatures and magnetic field orientations to probe the anisotropic response of the vortex lattice and its interaction with pinning landscapes intrinsic to the material.

The angular dependence of the torque signal reveals distinct signatures associated with vortex lattice melting, the crossover from three-dimensional to quasi-two-dimensional vortex behavior, and pinning-depinning transitions as functions of temperature and applied field strength. By analyzing the irreversible component of the torque as a function of field angle, we extract the critical current density and its anisotropy, providing insight into the effective mass tensor governing vortex motion along different crystallographic directions.

Measurements taken near the irreversibility line show a pronounced narrowing of the hysteretic torque response, consistent with thermally activated vortex creep and a weakening of pinning potentials as the sample approaches the normal state. Angular-dependent torque data further reveal evidence of a first-order vortex lattice melting transition, manifested as a sharp discontinuity in the torque curvature at specific field-temperature coordinates, in agreement with thermodynamic predictions for layered superconductors with strong anisotropy.

Comparison of torque results with complementary transport and magnetization measurements confirms the reliability of mechanical torque magnetometry as a sensitive probe of vortex matter phases. The high sensitivity of this technique to small changes in magnetic torque enables detection of subtle transitions in the vortex phase diagram that are often obscured in conventional resistive or SQUID-based measurements.

These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between vortex lattice elasticity, pinning disorder, and thermal fluctuations in high-temperature superconductors, and demonstrate the utility of torque magnetometry as a precise tool for mapping vortex phase diagrams and elucidating the microscopic mechanisms governing flux dynamics in strongly anisotropic superconducting systems.

# Abstract

We report a systematic investigation of threshold phenomena governing vortex lattice relaxation dynamics in isotropic high-temperature superconductors (HTSC) subjected to pulsed magnetic field perturbations. Through combined magneto-optical imaging and transport measurements on optimally-doped YBCO thin films with isotropic pinning landscapes, we identify a critical pulse duration τc below which vortex lattice reconfiguration is kinetically suppressed, resulting in negligible relaxation of the trapped flux density. For pulse durations exceeding τc, the system exhibits a pronounced transition to logarithmic relaxation behavior consistent with collective creep dynamics, with the relaxation rate S = -d(ln M)/d(ln t) increasing sharply across a narrow duration window (Δτ/τc ≈ 0.15). We attribute this threshold behavior to a competition between the characteristic depinning time of vortex bundles and the pulse duration, wherein sub-threshold pulses provide insufficient energy input to overcome local pinning barriers on timescales relevant to lattice reorganization. Temperature-dependent measurements (0.3Tc to 0.9Tc) reveal that τc scales with the thermal activation energy U0 according to τc ∝ exp(U0/kBT), suggesting the threshold originates from a activated escape process rather than a purely dynamic instability. Numerical simulations based on time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau theory, incorporating realistic pinning potential distributions, reproduce the observed threshold with quantitative agreement to experimental data across the explored parameter space. These findings establish pulse duration as a critical control parameter for engineering non-equilibrium vortex states and provide design criteria for pulsed-field magnetization protocols in superconducting bulk magnets, where precise control over trapped field profiles is essential for practical applications including compact motors, magnetic bearings, and levitation systems. Our results further suggest that threshold-duration engineering may offer a pathway to stabilizing metastable vortex configurations with enhanced critical current densities.

# Vortex Lattice Formation Time in HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ: Pulsed Field Studies

## Overview

Studies of vortex lattice formation dynamics in HoBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ (Ho-123) single crystals and textured samples using pulsed magnetic field techniques combined with mechanical relaxation (torque/vibrating reed) measurements have provided insight into the kinetics of flux penetration and the establishment of a metastable or equilibrium vortex configuration following rapid field changes.

## Key Experimental Approach

- **Pulsed field magnetization**: Fields are applied on millisecond timescales, allowing separation of fast electromagnetic penetration (governed by flux diffusion/critical state dynamics) from slower processes associated with vortex lattice reorganization.
- **Mechanical relaxation measurements**: Torque magnetometry or vibrating reed techniques probe the irreversible magnetic response and internal friction associated with vortex motion, providing a complementary dynamic signature of when the vortex system reaches a quasi-static configuration.

## Principal Findings

1. **Two-stage relaxation behavior**: The vortex system exhibits an initial fast response corresponding to flux front propagation (consistent with Bean critical-state dynamics) followed by a slower relaxation attributed to local rearrangement of vortices into a more ordered/pinned configuration.

2. **Formation time scale**: The characteristic time for the vortex lattice to reach a stable configuration after pulse application was found to lie in the range of **10⁻³–10⁻¹ s**, depending on temperature and field amplitude — much longer than the pulse rise time itself, indicating that vortex-vortex interactions and collective pinning effects dominate the late-stage relaxation.

3. **Temperature dependence**: As temperature increases toward T_c, the formation/relaxation time decreases due to reduced pinning barriers and enhanced thermally activated vortex motion (consistent with flux creep models).

4. **Correlation with mechanical dissipation**: Peaks in mechanical relaxation (internal friction) coincide with the intermediate timescale associated with vortex lattice reorganization, supporting the interpretation that the reed/torque response is sensitive to the same dissipative processes governing flux lattice ordering.

5. **Comparison with YBCO**: The vortex formation dynamics in Ho-123 are qualitatively similar to those in YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ, suggesting that rare-earth substitution (Ho for Y) does not significantly alter the fundamental pinning-controlled kinetics, consistent with the similar electronic structure and critical parameters of RE-123 compounds.

## Interpretation

The results support a picture in which vortex lattice formation after a field pulse is **not instantaneous** but proceeds through a pinning-controlled, thermally assisted relaxation process. The characteristic timescales extracted from pulsed field and mechanical measurements are consistent with flux creep/collective pinning theories, and they establish that mechanical techniques (torque, vibrating reed) provide a sensitive, complementary probe to conventional magnetometry for resolving vortex dynamics on sub-second timescales in high-T_c superconductors.

## Significance

These findings are relevant for:
- Understanding **flux dynamics** in bulk textured HTS materials used in engineering applications (e.g., trapped-field magnets).
- Establishing **design constraints** for pulsed-field magnetization protocols used to activate bulk superconductors.
- Providing experimental benchmarks for **theoretical models** of vortex lattice ordering and collective pinning in anisotropic high-temperature superconductors.

---

We study the dynamics of vortex matter in type-II superconductor under pulsed current excitation, with focus on how threshold pulse duration is affecting the formation of ordered vortex lattice structures. Using numerical simulation based on time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equations, we investigate the response of vortex system when subjected to current pulses of varying width and amplitude, for to understand the critical timescales that is governing transition from disordered vortex configuration to more ordered, lattice-like arrangement.

Our results are showing that there exist a well-defined threshold pulse duration, below which the vortex lattice cannot achieve sufficient ordering, regardless of how large is the pulse amplitude. This threshold is found to depend strongly on the vortex density and on pinning landscape of the sample. For pulse durations exceeding this threshold value, we observe the vortex lattice formation proceeding through several distinguishable stages: initial depinning of vortices from pinning centers, followed by rapid rearrangement into locally ordered domains, and finally the coarsening of these domains into large-scale hexagonal Abrikosov lattice.

The characteristic timescale for complete lattice formation is scaling with both the pulse amplitude and the strength of pinning potential, showing power-law behavior over the range of parameters that we have studied. These findings are providing new insight into the non-equilibrium dynamics of vortex matter and could have important implication for the design of superconducting devices where fast switching or pulsed operation is required, such as in superconducting digital electronics and vortex-based memory applications. The interplay between pulse duration, pinning strength, and lattice formation kinetics that we reveal here is suggesting new strategies for controlling vortex matter states through tailored pulse sequence, opening possibility for dynamic manipulation of vortex configurations in practical superconducting systems.
